clue.text: Left in van

blocks.note: the in thing is the one everybody likes, so in = popular
the van is the vanguard, the front of an army or a movement

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, no indicator and no join: the whole trick is that both halves are dictionary synonyms while the surface reads as a position on a road.
explanation.definitionFit: Left -> POPULAR FRONT: the standing name for a broad alliance of left-wing parties, after the French Front populaire of the 1930s.

clue.text: Could be Nepal one accepted – also separately Malta?

definitions.text: Could be Nepal one accepted – also separately Malta?

indicators.note: Saying a thing could be something else invites you to read the same letters as a different word entirely.

blocks.note: the country's own five letters, waiting to be re-sorted
the card accepted as one, high or low as the game decides, is the ace
taken on its own Malta is M, the letter its cars and aircraft carry

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: the two countries are examples of the answer and, with the ace and Malta's own letter, they are the letters you re-sort.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: Nepal is one and Malta another, while 'could be' admits the answer names the class rather than either country.

clue.text: ‘They’re on the house’ – worker comes in a lot

definitions.note: The setter defines by a whole sentence rather than a noun: 'they' stands in for the answer, and the barman's free round is the joke laid over the roof.

indicators.note: Whatever comes in has come inside the place named beside it, so those letters land within the other word instead of after it.

blocks.note: a lot of something is piles of it
the crossword's worker is almost always the ant

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the tell: they mark a phrase being quoted for its everyday meaning, and the everyday meaning is the wrong one.
explanation.definitionFit: ‘They’re on the house’ -> PANTILES: curved roofing tiles, which literally sit on top of a building — the free-drinks reading is the decoy.

clue.text: Decoy pocketing Charlie’s money

indicators.note: To pocket a thing is to slip it inside your coat, so the letter beside it disappears into the middle of the other word.

blocks.note: a decoy set out to draw something in is a lure
C is Charlie in the NATO alphabet, the same trick that makes Oscar an O

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drugs bust, where Charlie is cocaine; the wordplay only ever wanted the alphabet's third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: money -> LUCRE: the sneering word for money as gain, kept alive almost entirely by the phrase 'filthy lucre' out of the Epistle to Titus.

clue.text: Element from Red Planet

blocks.note: a steak still red in the middle is a rare one
the planet we are standing on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Planet' is Mars while you read it as a phrase and two unrelated words the moment you stop, which is why nothing here is about space.
explanation.definitionFit: Element -> RARE EARTH: the rare earths are the seventeen scandium and lanthanide metals, so the general word points at one particular family of them.

clue.text: Arrive in drag – men bowled over

indicators.note: Anyone bowled over has been knocked flat, and letters knocked flat like that finish up reading the opposite way.

blocks.note: to drag something along is to pull it
OR is other ranks, the army's men who are not officers

explanation.walkthrough: OR for other ranks is worth banking — it turns up far more often in cryptics than in life — and here it hides behind a picture of men in frocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrive -> ROLL UP: 'roll up!' is the fairground barker's call to come along, and the phrasal verb means to turn up, usually late or in numbers.

clue.text: Titled gent upset by journalist

indicators.note: Something upset has been tipped over, and in a down answer that means its letters are read from the bottom of the column upwards.

blocks.note: a gent is a man
ED is the editor, the journalist crosswords keep on the payroll

explanation.walkthrough: The aristocratic ring of 'titled' is pure decoy, and 'upset' has to be read as an instruction rather than as the gent's mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Titled -> NAMED: to be titled is to have been given a title, and a title is a name — the past participle, not anything to do with lords.

clue.text: Greedily handles fruit

indicators.note: Greed is never satisfied by one helping, so the word beside it is served up twice over.

blocks.note: to paw at something is to handle it clumsily
and again, because one grab was not enough

explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue with a doubling in it is Vlad at his most compact: the picture of grabby hands is also the instruction to take the word twice.
explanation.definitionFit: fruit -> PAWPAW: the other name for the papaya, the orange-fleshed tropical fruit, and in North America a different custard-like one entirely.

clue.text: Through Henry about to get free modern car

indicators.note: Turned about is turned to face the other way, so the two pieces before it are written in the opposite order to the one you read.

blocks.note: to go through a place is to go by way of it
H is the henry, the unit of electrical inductance
to get free of something is to be rid of it

explanation.walkthrough: Henry is a man in the surface and a unit of inductance in the wordplay — one of physics' quieter gifts to the crossword, alongside amp and ohm.
explanation.definitionFit: modern car -> HYBRID: the petrol-and-electric car, named from the general word for anything bred out of two different sources.

clue.text: With Adams’ header, win a second time

indicators.note: A footballer's header is played with the top of the head, and here it takes the letter sitting at the top of the name.

blocks.note: the letter at the front of Adams
to win something is to gain it

explanation.walkthrough: Tony Adams heading one in is the surface; the wordplay wants nothing of the man but his initial, which is what 'header' is quietly asking for.
explanation.definitionFit: a second time -> AGAIN: doing a thing again is doing it a second time, which is why the definition has to be a phrase rather than one word.

clue.text: Wow! Old political leader pointlessly filmed Harry entering

indicators.note: A point here is a point of the compass, N, so anything pointless has had that letter taken out of it.
To enter a building is to go inside it, so the name goes within the other word rather than alongside it.

blocks.note: Jeremy Corbyn, who led Labour until 2020
Harry Lime is the man everyone is hunting in The Third Man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cor blimey' is 'God blind me' worn smooth by a century of use, which is why it means nothing in particular and everything as an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Wow! -> COR BLIMEY: both are noises of pure astonishment rather than words with a sense, one of them wearing a Cockney accent.

clue.text: Trivial Pursuit’s first two getting egghead upset

indicators.note: Asking for the first two of a word takes the pair of letters at its start, still standing in the order they came.

blocks.note: the opening pair of letters of Pursuit
the head of egg is the letter at the top of it
to upset someone is to rile them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an instruction to turn something over and is a straight synonym instead, which is the whole trap in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Trivial -> PUERILE: not just unimportant but childishly so, the word carrying a sneer at whoever bothered with it that 'trivial' only implies.

clue.text: Expert fisherman, one might say, takes you round country

indicators.note: To carry something round is to move it about, and letters moved about like that do not stay in the order the clue set them.

blocks.note: an ace at anything is an expert at it
a river beat is let to so many rods, the angler named for his tackle
you is U, the letter that says the whole word

explanation.walkthrough: 'One might say' is Vlad owning how loose a rod for an angler is, and the fishing holiday it paints has nothing to do with South America.
explanation.definitionFit: country -> ECUADOR: the South American republic named after the equator running through it, so the general word points at one particular nation.

clue.text: Wives receiving ‘support’? No way, it’s a misleading term

indicators.note: To receive a guest is to have them into the house, so what is received sits inside rather than beside.

blocks.note: W is the standard shortening of wife, so two wives are two Ws
an easel is what supports a painter's canvas
no score at all is nothing, written as O
RD is road, the way on a street sign

explanation.walkthrough: 'No way' is a flat refusal in the surface and nothing-plus-road in the wordplay, and the quotation marks round support are the setter grinning.
explanation.definitionFit: a misleading term -> WEASEL WORD: one drained of meaning to dodge a commitment, from the weasel's trick of sucking an egg and leaving the shell whole.

clue.text: Powder, not drug – it’s right for treating medical condition

indicators.note: Putting 'not' in front of a thing takes that thing away from the letters you have been given.
To treat a substance is to work on it until it comes out changed, which is exactly what happens to these letters.

blocks.note: the word's own letters, before anything is done to them
E is the drug ecstasy, and it comes out of POWDER
the clue's own word, taken as its three letters
R is the standard shortening of right

explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface does double work: 'treating' is the instruction and 'condition' the definition, and they sit side by side pretending to be one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: medical condition -> WRIST-DROP: the limp hand left by damage to the radial nerve, a named clinical sign rather than a loose description.

clue.text: President departs, lying

blocks.note: Abe Lincoln, the president crosswords keep nearest to hand
D is departs on a timetable board

explanation.walkthrough: A first name and a station-board letter, wrapped in a surface about a president leaving office and telling untruths — neither of which is in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: lying -> ABED: to be abed is to be lying in bed, the old adverb that survives in 'up and abed' and hardly anywhere else.

clue.text: Playful lambs in SE showing soft and gentle nature

blocks.note: the word's own five letters
the clue's own word, taken as two letters rather than as a position
the compass point exactly as written

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a spring field and the only instruction in it is the first word; everything after it, small words included, is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: soft and gentle nature -> BALMINESS: the mildness of balmy air, the noun for weather that soothes — nothing to do with balmy meaning daft.

clue.text: Cunning hiding effect of injury – won leading decoration in battle

indicators.note: Something hidden is kept inside where it cannot be seen, so those letters go within the other word.
The leading letter is the one out in front of a word, and it is all that gets taken.

blocks.note: the letter at the front of won
art is cunning — the artful dodger's kind rather than the gallery's
what an injury leaves behind is pain

explanation.walkthrough: The dash tempts you to read 'won' with the first half of the clue; it belongs to the second, and until it moves there is no letter to start from.
explanation.definitionFit: decoration in battle -> WAR PAINT: the pattern daubed on the face before fighting, decoration in the sense of something applied rather than a medal.

clue.text: Try to get religious believer talking

indicators.note: Talking is saying rather than writing, so what counts is the noise a word makes, not the letters it is spelt with.

blocks.note: a Sikh is a believer in Sikhism, and his name is said exactly like the word wanted

explanation.walkthrough: Vlad is relying on you knowing how the religion is spelt: what you hear and what you write share not a single letter in the same place.
explanation.definitionFit: Try to get -> SEEK: to seek is to try to get hold of something, the verb at its plainest — seek and ye shall find.

clue.text: Writer’s copy almost ready for wrapping

indicators.note: Almost a word is not quite all of it, so the last letter never gets written down.
Wrapping paper closes round a parcel, so this piece goes round the letters it is handed.

blocks.note: ready is set — ready, steady, go — with the last letter gone
a crib is a copy to work from, the schoolboy's cheat sheet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' for SET is worth banking, and it explains a clue that otherwise looks as though it is about a manuscript nearly finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Writer -> SCRIBE: the copyist who wrote documents out by hand before printing, so the general word names one historical trade of writer.

clue.text: Run up to end something special

blocks.note: up in the air is high
the tail is the end of a thing — the tail of a queue, the tail of a plane
'it' was Clara Bow's word for the something extra a star has

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is American and never lets go of its 'it' — you cannot hightail anything else — which is why the last two letters need clueing separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Run -> HIGHTAIL IT: to hightail it is to leave at speed, from the deer that lifts its white tail as it bolts for cover.

clue.text: Iceland ordeal over, having a ball

blocks.note: an ordeal is a test, a trial you have to get through
IS is Iceland's international code, the letters on its cars and web addresses

explanation.walkthrough: Country codes are a small vocabulary that pays off often — E for Spain, D for Germany, IS here — and 'having a ball' sounds like a good holiday until the last word turns.
explanation.definitionFit: ball -> TESTIS: the clinical singular of what slang calls the balls, so a coarse everyday word defines the anatomist's one.

clue.text: Against describing one medic standing as blue-eyed boy

indicators.note: To describe a circle is to draw one round something, so this word goes around the letters that follow it.
Something standing has been set upright, and in a down answer upright means its letters are read from the bottom up.

blocks.note: the pros and cons are the fors and againsts
the Roman numeral for one
DR is the doctor, the crossword's standard medic

explanation.walkthrough: Two instructions sit next to each other here, one putting a piece inside and one turning the lot upright, and they have to be done in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: blue-eyed boy -> NORDIC: fair hair and blue eyes are the stock picture of the Scandinavian north, so the phrase describes a type rather than naming a favourite.

clue.text: Music and Liverpool? It’s a good relationship

blocks.note: rap is a kind of music
Liverpool is a port, and one of the great ones

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is covering a definition by example: any of Hull, Cork or Dover would have done the same job for those four letters.
explanation.definitionFit: a good relationship -> RAPPORT: the easy understanding between people who get on, borrowed from French and always used of the connection itself.

clue.text: Where to see pictures causing trouble with publicists?

blocks.note: PR is public relations, the publicists' trade
much ado is much trouble, as Shakespeare has it

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay describes a publicity disaster and the definition points at Madrid, and only the question mark warns that the two halves share no subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Where to see pictures -> PRADO: Madrid's national gallery, so a general phrase about paintings points at one particular building full of Goyas and Velázquezes.

clue.text: ‘Dead soldiers ultimately losers’ – Mr President regularly awful

indicators.note: What happens ultimately happens at the very end, so only the final letter of the word beside it is taken.
Doing a thing regularly is doing it at even intervals, so you pick every other letter as you go along.
An awful state is a mess, and letters in a mess are letters not yet in their proper order.

blocks.note: the final letter of losers
every other letter of Mr President, starting at the M

explanation.walkthrough: Two different letter-picking tricks feed a single anagram, so the order matters: choose the letters first, jumble them afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead soldiers -> EMPTIES: drinkers' slang for the bottles left standing when a party is over, which the drinks trade calls its empties.

clue.text: The bilingual church official

indicators.note: Someone bilingual has two languages, so the little word beside it is taken twice, once in each of them.

blocks.note: el is Spanish for the
der is German for the

explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords borrow the definite article from whichever language is handy — LE, LA, EL, DER, IL — and here one small word supplies the whole build.
explanation.definitionFit: church official -> ELDER: in Presbyterian and other reformed churches an elder is an ordained lay officer who helps govern the congregation.

clue.text: Wasted chance to go higher when retired?

blocks.note: to retire for the night is to go to bed
a ladder is a chance to get higher, up a wall or up a career

explanation.walkthrough: No word here tells you to put one piece inside the other — the single image of a ladder standing in the bedroom does that job, and its absence is the difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: Wasted -> BLADDERED: both are slang for very drunk, the British half of the pair naming the organ that a long evening's drinking fills.

clue.text: Old people’s home rejected jewellery originally

indicators.note: Something rejected is thrown back at you, so those letters are written the other way round.
What comes originally comes first of all.

blocks.note: ice is the jeweller's slang for diamonds
someone at home is in

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old people' is literal — a people, meaning a nation, rather than pensioners — and the surface's care home is there to stop you reading it that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Old people -> ICENI: Boudicca's tribe in East Anglia, so 'people' means a nation and 'old' means long vanished rather than elderly.

clue.text: Thieves disposed of mostly property and cash around island

indicators.note: To dispose things is to set them out in whatever order you choose, which is licence to re-set these letters.
Most of a word is all of it but the last letter, so one letter is left behind.

blocks.note: property with its final letter dropped
the word's own four letters
I is island on a map, and the other letters close around it

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a very new coinage and the wordplay is as old-fashioned as it comes, which is the joke: modern crime, Victorian machinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Thieves -> PORCH PIRATES: the recent name for people who steal delivered parcels off doorsteps, 'pirate' serving as the modern word for any casual robber.
